lesson.title: A Day in Berlin: Reading
lesson.subtitle: The full capstone passage — every word tap-to-inspectable, every shift annotated

hook.title: The Whole Passage
hook.content: Ein Tag in Berlin. Gestern waren der Mann und die Frau in der Stadt. Sie sind mit dem Zug gefahren — die Fahrt war kurz. In der Stadt haben sie Brot und Wasser gekauft, und das Brot war gut. Der Mann hat ein Buch gefunden — ein Buch über Berlin! Am Abend haben sie das Buch gelesen. Das Licht war warm, die Nacht war still. Heute trinken sie Kaffee im Haus. Mir ist kalt, sagt die Frau, aber es geht mir gut. Es gibt keinen besseren Morgen.

footnotes.title: The Annotated Word Count
footnotes.content: Roughly seventy words — and every single one has appeared in a lesson table or hint. The construction inventory: Perfekt brackets (haben gekauft/gelesen/gefunden), sein-perfects (sind gefahren), the simple past of sein (waren), dative receivers (mir), two-way prepositions (im Haus), a compound (impossible here — but Morgen/Brot carry their shifts), and a subordinate-free V2 spine throughout.

pattern.title: Read It Three Ways
pattern.content: Pass one — story: who did what, in order. Pass two — machinery: mark every verb position (V2 walls, bracket closures), every case flag (dem, der, mir), every umlaut. Pass three — production: cover the German, rebuild each sentence aloud from the English, then check. The passage is deliberately small: density is the test, not length. If you can rebuild 'Sie sind mit dem Zug gefahren' — sein for motion, mit + dative, nach-less city, participle last — you can build thousands of sentences no lesson ever taught you.
pattern.linguist_note: Notice the passage never uses the simple past except with war — because that is how spoken German actually works. The Perfekt brackets are the tense of real life; war is the fossil that survived.

exercises.prompt: Story order — match each beat with its line. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:

matching_pairs.german: Sie sind mit dem Zug gefahren
Sie haben Brot und Wasser gekauft

matching_pairs.english: The man found a book about Berlin
matching_pairs.german: Der Mann hat ein Buch über Berlin gefunden

matching_pairs.english: They read the book in the evening
matching_pairs.german: Am Abend haben sie das Buch gelesen

exercises.target_answer: Sie sind mit dem Zug gefahren, Sie haben Brot und Wasser gekauft, Der Mann hat ein Buch über Berlin gefunden, Am Abend haben sie das Buch gelesen, die Gabe, der Bauch, das Fieber, Wir müssen tun, das ist langweilig
exercises.meaning: They traveled by train; They bought bread and water; The man found a book about Berlin; They read the book in the evening; the gift; the belly; the fever; We must do; that is boring
exercises.explanation: Motion in sein-perfect, purchases in haben-perfect — the auxiliary logic running a real narrative.

exercises.prompt: Decode pass: which shift explains 'Nacht' in 'die Nacht war still'?
options: gh → ch — night's ghost letters still sounding
exercises.target_answer: gh → ch — night's ghost letters still sounding
exercises.meaning: Nacht ↔ night — the Atlas ghost map
exercises.explanation: The silent gh of night has been sounding in German for 1,300 years — and you can now hear it.

exercises.prompt: Grammar pass: 'Mir ist kalt, aber es geht mir gut' — how many dative experiencers?
options: Two: mir ist kalt and es geht mir gut
exercises.target_answer: Two: mir ist kalt and es geht mir gut
exercises.meaning: The dative experiencer twice in one breath
exercises.explanation: Cold happens TO her and the day goes TO her — the methinks grammar framing the story's feeling.

exercises.prompt: Production pass: which English word is 'kauf...' (in gekauft) hiding as a cousin?
exercises.explanation: Both from the Latin innkeeper/tradesman: English priced things cheap, German kept the verb kaufen.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "Yesterday the man and the woman were in the city"
exercises.target_answer: Gestern waren der Mann und die Frau in der Stadt
exercises.meaning: Yesterday the man and the woman were in the city

vocab_hints.note: in + dative for location: die Stadt → in der Stadt

exercises.explanation: Fronted time, plural waren, location dative (in der Stadt) — the opening sentence, rebuilt from parts you own.
exercises.idea: Yesterday the man and the woman were in the city
idea_parts: woman were in the city (verb in position 2)
cues: Start with "Gestern" and anchor "waren" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Read, decode, and rebuild the full capstone passage.
summary.takeaway: Seventy words, every construction from the trail — the reading is the diploma.

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

fahrt.etymology_derivation: Noun of fahren (fare): a 'faring' — a drive, ride, or voyage; the -t is the Germanic -þ nominal suffix. [wiktionary]

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

heute.etymology_derivation: Literally 'on this day': heu- is the he- of here/him, and the old ending hid Tag (day). English's own twin hēodæġ died out — today won. [wiktionary]

kaufen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, borrowed from Latin caupō 'tradesman/innkeeper' — the same loan that gave English cheap; collateral cognates. [wiktionary]
